I like to bemuse over certain subsets of gaming history from time to time and view it as a whole to understand where misconceptions or preconceptions come from. One of the least talked about but most fascinating subjects of gaming history for me are handhelds. My first handheld was the Gameboy Color and I have fond memories of playing Pokemon Red, Silver, and Platinum on it. However, handheld history tends to boil down to two things: Pokemon and Tetris.

It's easy to understand why this is. These two games definitely had a massive impact on all of game culture, to the point that even those in the "hardcore" crowd can't resist their allure. Is this really want handheld gaming amounted to though? "Downgraded console ports" and what would be called "casual" games? Obviously not, otherwise handhelds wouldn't be so worth talking about.

I do not draw a distinguishing line between games on given platforms. A handheld game can provide on as much complexity as a PC game (maybe going back a generation or so) and as much on an emotional level as a console game. The difference lies purely on the length of play. A truly effective handheld game should be able to perpetuate a reward cycle which is 10-30 min in length, as opposed to 1-5 min for mobile games (a topic for another time). The audience of console games though tend to enjoy binging, and thus a handheld experience seems far lessened when put into that context, thus handheld games are seen as "lesser by default".

However, all that is just me ranting about perception of games. What's really cool to look at is the hardware. Most just boil the history down to Mattel Auto Race, Milton Bradley Microvision, maybe Game & Watch, Game Boy, and Atari Lynx gets a cursory mention merely for being color. There were a lot more programmable handhelds than this though, and some of them are really quite intriguing. I assembled a list of them, because no single resource has all of these listed.

Bet you never knew the Philips CD-i had a handheld version. By far the most interesting out of these that I found was the Design Master Senshi Mangajukuu. It's kind of like the Playdia of handhelds, fitting as it was by Bandai. There are only two videos of it functioning on Youtube, both of the same game by Brazillians (I believe). While some may see the GameCom as the predecessor to the DS, I would wager that at least someone who started integrating the touch screen into the Game Boy Advance may have seen or heard about this device.

My point is that there's a lot about handheld history that's downright ignored, and collectors have very little interest in discovering the secrets of these machines. Notable exceptions include Laird's Lair, who has done many interviews with Atari Lynx devs; Ashens, who is a very funny and crude Youtuber who occasionally covers off-brand handhelds; and Sega-16, an all around great website that doesn't neglect the Sega handhelds. Of course, that means exploration of the major systems - the Game Boy line- are extremely limited, and gives the impression that this history isn't nearly as important.

Well that's a word you don't get to use every day! Its a very contentious word, one that stirs the mind when one puts it into a greater research context. We classify everything, so why is classifying genres so hard?

Obviously in the earliest days of these things called “video skill games” no one gave a second thought to what they might aspire to. Board games were just that, eventually evolving into “strategy” and “War games” being about as far as it went. Mechanical and electromechanical machines were classified by their make, not their core ideals. I think classification started to becoming a focus once racing games came into the equation in a bigger way, as there was no relating that sort of game to Pong, and that was about as simple as it ever got.

Following Space Invaders and the general diversification of gaming, you have an abundance of labels like “space shooters”, “munch mazes”, “climbing games”, and the like. All very inane concepts which were written by people coping with the phenomena.

There's always the argument for not having genres at all and letting things stand on their own merits. Obviously people like separation, but they also like unification. I think it's important to relate things, especially in art history, else you're left with nothing to stand on. Why would a title be so incredibly important if not for the fact that it was like other games that came after it? There are a few notable exceptions, but in all I think getting a grasp on genres as a concept is important for an audience to understand.

However, I am very much against some of the inane genre classification that goes on. I don't mind that people have differing ideals on these things, but that's not the case. It's frustratingly homongenized and dilutes actual classification. People have tried too hard to make games analogous to movies, and it's resulted in genre titles like action, adventure, and mystery.

What I believe genres should be about are the fundamental values of gameplay, and finding the line between certain genres should be an excersize in understanding play. This is one of the biggest periphery things I'm hoping to bring to my video series. I want to have this conversation more and not be the dictator of these terms. I'm not very good at coming up with names for things, and you can see that in my database.

One genre name that's become annoyingly and culturally ingrained is the term adventure. This can refer to three entirely different things. The first being “text adventures” which began with “Adventure”, and thus following games are “Adventure style games”. Not only does that completely bely the actual underlying themes of interactive fiction (the alternative term) as a whole, it also just adds to the confusion.

Most “scholarly types” use IF now, and yet they move the “Adventure” term over to games like Mystery House, despite the fact that mechanically they are the exact same game, just with added visual elements. Perhaps that speaks to that film aspect again, wherein sound films are entirely different than silent movies, but I don't believe this to be the case. For me it's “Visual Interactive Fiction”, and later terms I have yet to come up with. I don't dispute the use of “Point 'n click”, though I'm trying to avoid using it as a genre definition in this history.

Finally, there's the “Adventure” defined by Warren Robinett's Adventure. The Zelda/Metroid like game, AKA “Action-adventure”. This is where things get very tricky. Yes, adventuring is a core aspect of these games. Is it really the act of adventuring though, or of discovery? I think there's an important distinguishing line there, though that's a topic for another time. Suffice to say, I don't like shifting this vague term of “Adventure” all over the place. It just leads to confusion and dis-satisfactory means of explaining related games. Time to pull out the old quote machine to show you what I'll be presenting people with.

Do I seem contradictory for approving of the term “Roguelike” whilst dismissing the term “Adventure” for two different genres based on the names of their progenitors? Maybe I do, but the term “Adventure” is simply too generic to exist within the terms of defining video game genres. Games are not categorized like movies which reflect on the thematic qualities they present in furthering a narrative. “Adventure” is a tag slapped onto action movies with scope, and even film came up with a more nuanced literary parallel by adopting the term “Epic” for certain movies that could be seen as “Adventure” films. Though I know it'll probably just be a nuisance for some people, one of my intents with this series was to open up those terms a bit more and help define these games beyond what they have historically been called. My term for these types of games, which is totally non-concise and a work in progress, will for the remainder of this history be: Exploratory Item-Gathering game.

Specifically, Adventure is a Self-Contained Exploratory Item-Gathering game. This means that the limits of the world are clearly defined, and the fact that much of it is arranged in corridors, taking advantage of confined space, gives the player an impression that the scope of the world is limited. It's slightly to do with thematic elements, but it really does make an impression on the game itself, separating the two big parallels in “Action Adventure” games that will be covered eventually. The bridge which allowed players to get through walls loosened up the confines a little bit though. At its core, Atari Adventure was a game about collecting and discovering items, then using wits and skill to bring the item to a specific place. There was no ambiguity of parser input such as in the Crowther and Woods game or strict puzzles to solve. Get the key from A to B and deal with hazards along the way using other items, then get the big item and bring it to the end. That basic structure would become the crux of this new genre.

So yes, I have two separate terms here, since I believe there is a very distinguishable quality between the paths set by Metroid and Zelda. I will talk about those when the time comes, but now I leave it to you all.

Are genres ultimately superfluous in discussion of overall history? Should we really be trying to find links between games mechanically?

Should definitions of this nature be colloquial?

What do you think of the term “first person shooter”?
